subject: Unreal Editor
scope: Standalone generic editor product model, project code integration, authoring workflows, play execution, extensions, and failure/version behavior relevant to a Rust-first Nara editor.

primary_editor_entry.summary: The normal product is a generic Unreal Editor application that opens a .uproject through the launcher, project browser, file association, or command line. Unreal does not normally ask each project to own a separately designed editor application. Native C++ projects nevertheless need compatible project modules built for an Editor target before project-defined native types and tools can participate in that generic editor process.

findings.claim: The user-facing editor shell is engine-owned and project-generic; the project supplies a descriptor, content, configuration, modules, and plugins rather than its own editor UI executable.

Blueprint-only and content-centric work can remain inside the generic editor without compiling project C++ for each asset edit. Adding native project code changes the requirement: UnrealBuildTool creates project targets and the project must have an Editor-target build for its C++ changes to appear in Unreal Editor.

A C++ project therefore does compile project-specific Editor-target artifacts, but this is not the same product model as compiling and launching a bespoke project editor. The generic UnrealEditor process loads compatible project and plugin modules.

For Nara, the important product invariant is the standalone generic nara-editor executable. Project-specific compilation may enrich schemas, behaviors, and tools, but it must not be required merely to launch the editor, browse assets, inspect raw scene structure, or repair a project.

first_open_and_iteration.summary: Unreal separates lightweight project/content discovery from loading every object, then offers several iteration loops: data and Blueprint edits inside the editor, material and asset recompilation, native Live Coding, and full rebuild/restart when structural changes exceed the safe live-patch envelope.

findings.claim: The Asset Registry asynchronously gathers metadata about unloaded assets and makes that inventory searchable without loading every asset. This is central to acceptable first-open and content-browser behavior on large projects.
Derived data is treated as disposable cache output that can be regenerated from source assets; it is not the sole authoring source of truth.

Blueprints give designers an in-editor code-like iteration path over reflected engine and project types, while C++ changes can use Live Coding to rebuild and patch binaries while the editor or PIE is running.

Live Coding is not magic schema independence. It relies on Object Reinstancing for reflected structural changes, has pointer/cache cleanup obligations, does not update existing instances for every constructor-default change, and can still require a clean restart or full rebuild for reliable recovery.

The productive experience comes from multiple bounded iteration lanes, not from forcing every edit through the native compiler. Nara should make scene, UI, animation, material, and declarative tool edits compiler-free, with Rust compilation reserved for runtime logic or native extension changes.

authoring_coverage.summary: Unreal presents a family of domain editors within one product: level/scene editing, Details inspection, visual scripting, UI layout, materials, animation/rigging, sequenced cinematics, asset import/reimport, debugging, and packaging. These tools share the project, asset registry, reflection, selection, transaction, and viewport infrastructure while retaining domain-specific editors.

findings.claim: Scene authoring is centered on the Level Editor viewport, hierarchy/outliner, content browser, transform gizmos, and the reflected Details panel rather than on editing raw runtime objects directly.

UI authoring uses Widget Blueprint assets with a visual Designer and a Graph for behavior, demonstrating that layout data and behavior logic can have different authoring surfaces while remaining one asset workflow.

Materials are first-class assets edited in a node graph, compiled with localized errors, and previewed live. Shader authoring is therefore a domain product with a graph, compiler diagnostics, preview viewport, and asset lifecycle, not just a generic property panel.
Control Rig and Sequencer provide in-engine rigging and animation workflows, including dedicated assets, controls, constraints, debugging, and Python extension points.

Import and reimport are explicit content-pipeline operations. The Interchange framework separates translators, pipelines, source data, and generated engine assets rather than treating imported cache output as an opaque manual copy.

For Nara, Scene View, Game View, UI Designer, Animation/Timeline, Material/Shader Graph, asset browser, inspector, diagnostics, and build/run are product domains sharing an editor shell. They should not be collapsed into one universal widget toolkit abstraction.

persistent_data_model.summary: Unreal combines a generated reflection system with serialized UObject assets and packages. Source assets, imported engine assets, asset metadata, compiled Blueprint state, and rebuildable derived data have distinct roles. Version and custom-version metadata participate in load/save compatibility.

findings.claim: UHT parses Unreal-specific metadata in C++ headers, generates UObject support code, and runs before the C++ compiler under UnrealBuildTool. UCLASS, USTRUCT, UFUNCTION, UPROPERTY, enum, delegate, and related metadata become the common schema substrate for serialization, editor property exposure, Blueprint integration, and runtime identity.
Assets are UObject-based serialized records stored in packages such as .uasset and .umap. Asset Registry tags provide a compact discovery/index layer that can be queried while assets remain unloaded.

Blueprints, materials, animation rigs, sequences, and widgets are durable authoring assets. Their executable or GPU-ready forms are compiled or derived from those assets rather than replacing the authoring source.

Engine version, serialization version, Build ID, and GUID-based custom versions are explicit compatibility mechanisms. Newer assets are intentionally not generally safe to open and resave in older editors; Epic documents concrete data-loss hazards when incompatible assets disappear and references become null.

Nara should adopt the separation of durable source documents, queryable asset metadata, generated/compiled artifacts, and disposable caches. It should not reproduce Unreal's lossy behavior for unknown or unavailable fields; Nara's source document should preserve unknown records byte-for-byte or prohibit saving them.

project_code_loading.summary: Native project and plugin code is organized into UnrealBuildTool modules and loaded into the editor according to target type and loading phase. Blueprint logic is stored as project content and executed through Unreal's reflected scripting stack. The model achieves deep integration but binds native extensions to the exact engine/module ABI and editor process.

findings.claim: Projects and plugins declare modules in .uproject/.uplugin descriptors. Runtime and Editor module types control where code may load, while Build.cs and Target.cs define compilation and dependency closure.
Code plugins contain compiled binaries, can declare reflected types, and are compiled as dependencies of the project when source is present. Editor modules load when the editor starts.

Blueprints provide a lower-friction project logic and extension lane but depend on reflected native types and engine-owned runtime/editor services. They reduce native compilation frequency; they do not eliminate the native substrate.

Unreal's native modules are loaded in the editor process. The absence of a documented general sandbox or process boundary for arbitrary Editor modules means a faulty native extension shares the editor's memory and crash domain; this is an architectural inference from the module-loading model, not an explicit Epic reliability guarantee.

Nara should not make Rust dynamic libraries the primary project-schema mechanism: Rust has no stable language ABI comparable to the tightly controlled same-version C++/engine module contract Unreal assumes. Nara should instead load a versioned declarative schema bundle for authoring and use a separately built project process for executable behavior.

play_execution_model.summary: Unreal supports rapid in-editor preview and explicit outside-editor execution. PIE and SIE provide different control semantics; selected viewport and new editor window are editor-integrated modes, while Standalone Game runs outside the editor. Play state is transient by default, with an explicit operation to keep selected simulation changes.

findings.claim: PIE can start immediately without first packaging a standalone application, and offers pause, frame advance, stop, eject, possess, console, and multiple viewport/window modes.
SIE runs simulation without spawning/possessing the normal player, making it a distinct authoring/debugging tool rather than merely another launch flag.
Standalone Game launches outside the editor, while New Editor Window remains a PIE mode. This gives users a deliberate fidelity-versus-iteration choice.

Edits made to play/simulation objects are not durable by default; Keep Simulation Changes is explicit. This protects the authoring document from accidental mutation while still permitting selective capture.
Live Coding can patch native code during editor work, PIE, or an attached packaged desktop build, but restart/full rebuild remains part of the correctness model.

Nara's first credible Play implementation should build and run a project-owned game executable as a child process, stream diagnostics and lifecycle state into the generic editor, and preserve the editor document as authority. Embedded Game View can be added behind an explicit transport/lease contract after external Play is reliable.

editor_extension_model.summary: Unreal offers an extension ladder from data-only content and Blueprint/Python utilities to deeply integrated native Editor modules. Native plugins can add types, menus, toolbars, modes, tabs, Details customizations, importers, asset editors, component visualizers, gizmos, and interactive tools.

findings.claim: Plugins are discoverable project/engine packages of code and data that can be enabled per project and can extend runtime features, editor menus, toolbar commands, sub-modes, and file types.
IDetailCustomization and IPropertyTypeCustomization let native extensions replace or augment how reflected objects and property types appear in the Details panel.
ToolMenus, Slate tab spawners, Editor Utility Widgets, and Python provide several levels for adding menus, commands, dockable tabs, dialogs, and workflow utilities.
The Interactive Tools Framework and component visualizers provide reusable input, selection, gizmo, viewport overlay, and tool-lifecycle infrastructure for domain-specific scene tools.
Factories, AssetTools, and Interchange translators/pipelines support new asset types and import/reimport workflows, while custom asset editors can provide domain-specific tabs and previews.

Nara should likewise define a graded extension model: declarative schema and property metadata first; data-authored editor panels/actions second; isolated tool processes or a stable sandboxed guest ABI for advanced extensions third; trusted in-process Rust extensions only as an explicit expert mode, not the default project requirement.

failure_and_versioning_model.summary: Unreal makes module and asset compatibility explicit, uses versioned serialization and redirect/migration facilities, treats derived data as rebuildable, and provides crash reporting/recovery tooling. Its native extension model nevertheless has a broad in-process failure domain, and its documented incompatible-asset behavior includes cases where resaving can lose references.

findings.claim: Engine/module Build IDs and compatible versions determine whether binaries may load. Plugin descriptors identify modules, target types, loading phases, versions, and expected binaries.
Custom serialization versions allow parallel domain migrations, while Core Redirects support renamed classes, structs, enums, functions, properties, and packages.

Epic explicitly warns that assets from incompatible newer versions may not appear, references may be treated as null, and saving the referring asset can lose information. This is a cautionary example for Nara: unavailable schema must never silently become deletion authority.

Crash reporting captures diagnostics after engine crashes, while Disaster Recovery provides an editor recovery module around transaction synchronization. These mitigate failure aftermath rather than isolating arbitrary native plugins from the editor process.

Nara should encode project schema fingerprint, engine/editor compatibility, document format version, migration lineage, and extension protocol version separately. A missing executable module must degrade executable previews/tools, not make durable scene records unknown-and-discardable.

strengths.summary: Unreal's productivity comes from a stable editor product, a unified reflected asset universe, specialized authoring tools, several iteration speeds, and an extension ladder that serves artists, technical designers, and C++ programmers.

findings.claim: One editor shell keeps project browsing, scene editing, asset management, domain editors, build, play, diagnostics, and packaging coherent.
Generated reflection provides enough structure to produce generic Details inspection while still supporting bespoke editors and customizations.
Blueprint, asset, material, animation, and UI edits avoid the full native compile loop, while Live Coding reduces C++ iteration latency when native changes are necessary.
PIE/SIE/Standalone modes recognize that fastest iteration and final runtime fidelity are different product needs.

weaknesses.summary: The same depth that makes Unreal productive also creates heavy coupling: generated reflection, module build/version requirements, broad native plugin privileges, complex object reinstancing, binary asset/version constraints, and substantial implementation surface.

findings.claim: Native types and editor plugins remain tied to UHT, UBT, Editor targets, module descriptors, matching binaries, and engine Build IDs.
Live Coding carries correctness limits and cleanup obligations; structural replacement can invalidate pointers and caches and may crash when contracts are violated.
Native Editor modules run with deep in-process access, so extension power and failure blast radius are coupled.
Asset compatibility policy prevents unsafe backward opening but can make incompatible assets disappear and can still permit destructive resaves of references if the user proceeds carelessly.

Replicating UObject, UHT, Blueprint VM, Slate, asset registry, import pipeline, PIE, material compiler, animation suite, and plugin surface all at once would overwhelm Nara and delay a usable product.

nara_transferable_lessons.summary: Nara should copy Unreal's product shape and separation of authoring sources from derived execution artifacts, adapt reflection and extension loading for Rust's constraints, and reject compile-to-view and unrestricted in-process native extension requirements.
copy: Ship a stable standalone nara-editor executable with a project browser and recent-project workflow; a CLI may forward to it but is not the primary product.
Use a queryable project asset index so the editor can discover and classify content without fully materializing every asset.

Treat scenes, prefabs, UI documents, animation timelines, material graphs, and editor layouts as durable authoring documents; treat GPU packets, imported caches, thumbnails, and runtime lowering as rebuildable artifacts.
Provide a common selection, transaction, undo/redo, command, diagnostics, asset reference, and viewport tool substrate, then build domain-specific editors on top.
Offer distinct Edit, Simulate, Play, and External Run semantics, with play-state changes transient unless explicitly applied back through an authoring transaction.
Offer an extension ladder so many custom workflows do not require native code.
adapt: Replace UHT/UObject coupling with a versioned Nara authoring schema bundle generated from Rust declarations or source metadata. The generic editor consumes this bundle without loading the project's Rust binary.

Keep the last valid schema bundle as an editor cache, but bind it to a project/source fingerprint and visibly mark staleness. Opening remains possible; execution and schema-sensitive writes can be gated.

When a schema is unavailable, preserve unknown component envelopes losslessly and limit unsafe field edits instead of treating the component as absent. Complete-schema-only projects may choose a hard read-only gate, but not lossy save.

Run project gameplay in an external child process first. Use a versioned IPC protocol for lifecycle, diagnostics, selection/picking, hot data reload, and later frame transport. Do not block the initial editor on embedded GPU sharing.

Implement custom inspectors primarily as declarative field presentation, validation, actions, and Nara UI documents. Host advanced Rust editor tools out of process or behind a future stable/sandboxed guest ABI.

Separate project format version, schema identity, runtime build identity, editor extension protocol, and imported artifact version so one mismatch does not invalidate unrelated authoring capabilities.
reject: Do not require every Rust project to compile a project-specific editor executable merely to view a scene.
Do not make loading arbitrary Rust dynamic libraries into nara-editor the default schema or plugin mechanism; Rust ABI instability and in-process crash scope make this an unsuitable foundation.
Do not reproduce UObject as a single object model owning persistence, runtime identity, reflection, garbage collection, scripting, and editor identity.
Do not silently drop unknown components or fields when code/schema is missing or newer than the editor.
Do not attempt Live Coding-style native object reinstancing in the first editor product. Prefer deterministic external rebuild/restart and data-state handoff.
Do not place all specialized authoring behavior into a universal UI toolkit or generic Inspector; material, animation, UI, and scene tools need explicit domain models.

minimum_viable_path.summary: The smallest credible path preserves the mature product experience without rebuilding Unreal: a generic editor that can always open and repair source documents, a generated non-executable schema catalog, a reliable external Play loop, a few complete domain authoring slices, and a deliberately constrained extension model.

phases.name: Generic standalone project opening
deliverables: nara-editor.exe owns project selection, recent projects, open/close, workspace layout, diagnostics, and recovery.
Project opening reads nara.toml, source asset inventory, document headers, and the last compatible authoring schema bundle without compiling project Rust code.
Scene hierarchy, stable identities, transforms, raw component envelopes, asset references, and diagnostics remain visible even when some schemas are missing.
Unknown records are losslessly retained; unsafe documents are read-only or only allow schema-independent structural edits.

phases.name: Versioned authoring schema pipeline
deliverables: A build-time Rust schema exporter emits a deterministic, versioned, non-executable catalog containing component/type IDs, fields, defaults, constraints, enum choices, units, resource kinds, migration IDs, inspector hints, and action descriptors.
The catalog is committed or cached according to an explicit project policy and carries source, toolchain, engine, and composition fingerprints.
The editor compares current project state with the catalog and offers Generate/Refresh Schema as a build task; stale schema does not prevent basic project opening.
Runtime startup performs a schema fingerprint handshake so the editor cannot pretend that a stale catalog matches the running game.

phases.name: Complete scene and property editing slice
deliverables: Scene Tree, selection, Inspector, transform gizmo, prefab instance/source navigation, save, undo/redo, validation, source-control-safe writes, and actionable missing-schema diagnostics form one end-to-end workflow.
Reference Game and a generated starter consume the identical generic editor path; neither owns editor UI code.
A schema-provided custom presentation can change labels, ranges, grouping, visibility, validation, and bounded actions without native editor code.

phases.name: External Play and Game View lifecycle
deliverables: The editor invokes Cargo through a controlled build service, parses structured diagnostics, and starts/stops/restarts the project game process.
Edit documents remain authoritative; runtime state is isolated and discarded on Stop unless the user executes an explicit Apply Runtime Changes transaction.
The first release uses an external game window. A later Game View adds a versioned frame/input/resize lease without changing project composition or schema ownership.
Build failure, game crash, protocol mismatch, and stale schema leave the editor alive with repair actions.

phases.name: First-party domain productivity
deliverables: Add one complete UI authoring workflow and one complete animation or material workflow, including preview, diagnostics, save, undo, and runtime consumption.
Treat shader compilation, asset import, thumbnails, and runtime lowering as cancellable jobs with retained last-good output.
Persist editor layout and project-local tool configuration as data so ordinary workspace customization requires no compilation.

phases.name: Constrained editor extensions
deliverables: Data-authored Nara UI panels, commands, menus, inspector metadata, validators, import recipes, and action RPC cover common project customization.
Advanced Rust extensions run in a supervised tool process with a capability-scoped, versioned protocol where feasible; a crash retires the tool session, not the editor document authority.
Only after real extensions prove the need should Nara consider a stable guest ABI such as WebAssembly or a trusted in-process native tier.

non_goals_for_first_release: Native Rust live binary patching and object reinstancing
Arbitrary in-process Rust editor plugin loading
Embedded multi-viewport GPU sharing before external Play is reliable
A universal importer framework before two real asset domains require it
Parity with Unreal's complete animation, material, cinematic, and modeling suites
minimum_viable_path.success_criterion: A user downloads or builds nara-editor once, opens a starter or Reference Game without compiling a bespoke editor, views and edits source scenes safely, changes reflected values, saves/undoes, presses Play, receives actionable build/runtime diagnostics, stops the game without destabilizing the editor, and can reopen the same project even when project code or an optional tool extension no longer builds.

primary_sources.title: Compiling Game Projects
supports: UnrealBuildTool uses Build.cs and Target.cs files.
Projects have Editor, Game, Client, and Server targets.
A project must be built with an Editor target to open in Unreal Editor with project code changes reflected.

primary_sources.title: Unreal Engine Modules
supports: Modules encapsulate runtime features and editor tools as separate compilation units.
.uproject and .uplugin descriptors control module type and loading phase.
Runtime and Editor are distinct common module types, and modules can be loaded/unloaded by the host.

primary_sources.title: Unreal Header Tool
supports: UHT parses C++ header metadata and generates code for the UObject system before C++ compilation.
UHT exposes the parsed package/type tree to exporters.
Reflected keywords and property types are deeply integrated with generated engine code.

primary_sources.title: Objects in Unreal Engine
supports: UObject-derived types participate in reflection, serialization, editor integration, and garbage collection.
UCLASS and UPROPERTY metadata determine engine-visible type and property behavior.

primary_sources.title: Asset Registry
supports: The registry gathers information about unloaded assets asynchronously.
Asset metadata/tags can be queried without fully loading every asset.

primary_sources.title: Asset Management
supports: Unreal assets are UObject-based project content identified and managed through engine asset systems.
Primary and secondary asset identities support discovery and loading policy.

primary_sources.title: Derived Data Cache
supports: Derived data is generated from source assets and can be regenerated.
Local/shared/cloud cache layers reduce repeated processing without becoming authoring authority.

primary_sources.title: Versioning of Assets and Packages
supports: Engine Version, serialization versions, Build ID, and GUID-based custom versions govern compatibility.
Incompatible newer assets may not appear and references may be treated as null.
Saving after an incompatible load can lose information, which Epic explicitly warns against.

primary_sources.title: Core Redirects
supports: Redirects support renamed classes, structs, enums, functions, properties, and packages during migration.

primary_sources.title: Blueprints Visual Scripting
supports: Blueprints provide a node-based in-editor scripting and asset-authoring environment.
Blueprint exposure builds on reflected engine and project types.

primary_sources.title: Live Coding
supports: Live Coding rebuilds and patches C++ binaries while the editor, PIE, or an attached packaged desktop build is running.
Object Reinstancing replaces reflected instances for structural changes.
Reinstancing has pointer/cache cleanup requirements and documented crash risks.

primary_sources.title: Playing and Simulating
supports: PIE and SIE provide distinct preview semantics without packaging first.
Selected Viewport, New Editor Window, and Standalone Game are distinct play modes.
Simulation changes are transient unless explicitly kept.

primary_sources.title: Plugins
supports: Plugins can contain code and content and can extend runtime and editor functionality.
Plugins can add menus, toolbar commands, modes, file types, and reflected types.
Code plugin modules are compiled with the project and expected binaries load at editor startup.

primary_sources.title: FPluginDescriptor API
supports: Plugin descriptors carry version, engine compatibility, module, platform, and enablement metadata.

primary_sources.title: IDetailCustomization API
supports: Native extensions can customize the Details layout for reflected object classes.

primary_sources.title: IPropertyTypeCustomization API
supports: Native extensions can customize header and child presentation for reflected property types.

primary_sources.title: UToolMenus API
supports: Editor extensions can register and extend menus and toolbars through a shared service.

primary_sources.title: Editor Utility Widgets
supports: Project tools can be authored as UMG-based editor tabs and utilities without implementing a complete native editor module UI.

primary_sources.title: Scripting the Unreal Editor Using Python
supports: Python can automate editor tasks and content pipelines as a lower-friction extension lane.

primary_sources.title: Interactive Tools Framework
supports: The framework provides reusable input, tool lifecycle, property sources, rendering, and gizmo infrastructure for interactive editor tools.

primary_sources.title: FComponentVisualizer API
supports: Editor extensions can draw and interact with component-specific visualizations in viewports.

primary_sources.title: Interchange Framework
supports: Import/reimport is decomposed into source data, translators, pipelines, and generated engine assets.

primary_sources.title: Material Editor Guide
supports: Materials are node-graph assets with compile/save/apply workflow.
The editor provides live previews, shader recompilation controls, and localized compiler errors.

primary_sources.title: Control Rig
supports: Unreal provides in-engine rigging and animation tools, dedicated Control Rig assets, Sequencer integration, debugging, and Python extension.

primary_sources.title: UMG UI Designer User Guide
supports: Widget Blueprint authoring combines a visual layout designer with graph-based behavior editing.

primary_sources.title: Unreal Editor Interface
supports: The main editor integrates viewport, toolbar, outliner, Details panel, content drawer, and dockable domain tools.

primary_sources.title: Crash Reporting
supports: Crash reports capture call stacks, system information, logs, and optional user context after a crash.

primary_sources.title: IDisasterRecoveryClientModule API
supports: Unreal ships a dedicated Disaster Recovery client module backed by transaction synchronization infrastructure.

uncertain: Epic's public documentation does not specify one universal UI flow for every combination of missing, stale, or incompatible project module and plugin binary. Exact prompts and automatic rebuild behavior vary by installed/source engine, platform, IDE integration, and engine version.

The claim that arbitrary native Editor plugin faults can crash the whole editor is a strong architectural inference from in-process module loading, not an explicit Epic guarantee about every plugin or failure class.
Blueprint VM bytecode layout, load-time compilation details, and internal editor object-reinstancing implementation are intentionally not characterized beyond Epic's public contracts.
First-open latency, Live Coding latency, asset indexing throughput, and plugin crash frequency are not compared quantitatively because no reproducible official benchmark was found.

The public documentation does not establish a general lossless placeholder contract for assets whose defining native class or plugin is completely unavailable. Nara should make this behavior explicit rather than infer it from Unreal.

Some Epic documentation URLs are version-neutral and currently resolve to Unreal Engine 5.8; exact UI labels and experimental status can change between minor releases without changing the architectural findings.
